text.content: Defining a single-agent architecture

rich_text.plain_text: Defining a single-agent architecture

text.content: In a single-agent pattern, one language model acts as the central reasoning engine for all tasks. It handles every query through the same model, the same memory, and the same toolset. Every request enters the same reasoning loop and exits through the same response generation step.

text.content: Debugging:

rich_text.plain_text: Debugging:

text.content: When the agent produces an unexpected response, there is one chain of reasoning to inspect. The prompt, the retrieved chunks, the tool output, and the generated response are all part of a single, traceable sequence. In a multi-agent system, the same failure might involve three or four agents passing state between each other, any one of which could be the source of the problem.

text.content: Cost predictability:

rich_text.plain_text: Cost predictability:

text.content: A single agent makes a bounded number of language model calls per query. The token consumption per interaction is predictable and manageable. Multi-agent systems can consume ten to fifteen times more tokens for the same underlying task because coordination, delegation, and synthesis all require additional model calls.

text.content: Takeaway:

rich_text.plain_text: Takeaway:

text.content: The correct starting point for any agent architecture is the simplest system that can solve the problem reliably. A single agent with well-configured memory, retrieval, and tools handles the majority of business use cases at lower cost, lower latency, and higher debuggability than a multi-agent alternative. For Contigo's support agent as built in this course, no such gap exists. The single-agent Chatflow with memory, retrieval, and tools is the correct and sufficient architecture.
